folder.name: Kitchen Essentials and Basic Food Preparation

sets.name: Basic Food Preparation and Technique
sets.description: Mise en place, knife safety and parts, cutting and chopping styles, measuring techniques, mixing techniques, and seasonings, flavorings, marinating, and brining.

terms.definition: A French culinary word which means "Everything put in place." Refers to the practice of preparing and organizing all ingredients and equipment before cooking. It's a crucial concept in professional kitchens, ensuring a smooth and efficient cooking process. This involves tasks like chopping vegetables, measuring spices, and arranging everything in an organized manner.

terms.term: How to Properly Use Mise en Place
terms.definition: Have your recipe handy and develop a plan. Gather all of your ingredients, utensils, and equipment needed. One by one, wash, cut, dice, chop, and measure all of your ingredients. Place them into appropriately sized dishes, bowls, and containers for easy grabbing. Set your ingredients around your cooking station for better accessibility. For a larger-scale cooking project, you can place all of your cold ingredients in containers that fit in a commercial refrigerator to easily grab from as you cook.

A sharp knife is a safe knife. Using a dull knife is an invitation to disaster — if you try to force a dull knife through the surface of a food product, it is more likely to slip and cause an injury. Never, ever grab a falling knife; the best way to avoid having to think about this rule is to make sure your knife is always completely on your work surface, without the handle sticking out into traffic areas. Use the right knife for the right job. Always cut away from — never towards — yourself. When you have a knife, keep your eyes on the blade. Carry a knife properly. Never, ever put a knife in a sink full of water. Always cut on a cutting board — never on wooden tables — and do not cut on metal, glass, or marble, as this will ultimately damage a knife's edge.

terms.term: The 12 Parts of a Kitchen Knife

terms.definition: The end of the blade. It serves to create a pivot point used in several different cutting methods, and includes the knifepoint.
The portion of the blade between the tip and heel. Knives with "curvy" bellies and small tips are good for chopping vegetables, as they allow quick and smooth cutting motions.
The end of the blade just before the handle, opposite the tip. Some blades have the heel blended into an extended bolster for more protection at the cost of versatility.
Its primary function is to add strength where the handle joins the blade.
The back of the blade, opposite the cutting edge.
The front part of the knife. It is used for scoring and piercing.
The cutting part of the blade. It is used for chopping and slicing.
The butt, or pommel, serves as a reference point for the hand.

Also called the French knife, it is the most frequently used knife in the kitchen. The positioning of the grip and of the food under the blade both influence the degree of control and leverage a person has over it.

Grasp the blade firmly between the pad of the thumb and the knuckle of the index finger, just in front of the bolster, curling the remaining fingers around the bottom of the handle. Curl the fingers of the guiding hand inward for protection. A good grip allows the user to control the movement of the knife, avoiding slippage. Resist the temptation to extend the index finger along the spine of the knife, because that method results in a lack of control of the angle being worked with.
Cutting of food into large or thin pieces. The base of the knife is lifted up and down with a forward and backward motion.
This cut looks like a matchstick and has the nickname "shoestring." It is also a good size for cutting potatoes for French fries. A julienne of potato is sometimes referred to as an allumette.
To cut leaf vegetables into thin strips.
To cut food into even-size cubes (1/8 to 1/4 inch).
To chop food into very fine pieces (less than 1/8 inch).

Means "little ribbons" in French. This cut is mainly used for vegetable leaves and fresh herbs, in particular basil. The leaves are stacked, rolled, and then sliced perpendicularly, creating thin strips.
To cut food into even-size cubes (about 1/2 inch).
Uneven cutting of foods into small pieces (less than 1/4 inch), or a coarse chop with 1/2 or 3/4 inch irregular pieces.

To cut off the outer coating (peel) of vegetables or fruits. Squaring off, or "parer" in French, is the first step for creating most of the classic cuts. The first step in squaring off is to cut the product into roughly 2 to 2 1/2 inch segments.
Measures 5 mm on each side, which makes it the smallest of the dice cuts. Brunoise is usually used for garnishes.
A French cooking term used to describe a style of cutting vegetables which means "country-style." It consists of slices of vegetables about 1 mm thick.
A vegetable cut into batons or sticks. Batonnet, or baton, is a matchstick knife cut with precise dimensions of about 1/4 inch by 1/4 inch, and roughly 2 to 2 1/2 inches long.
A French cooking term meaning to cut a vegetable into thickish batons. This is the size of vegetables commonly used in frozen vegetable mixes.

A French cooking term for a mixture of vegetables. The vegetables should be chopped into cubes 4 mm x 4 mm x 4 mm (1/6th inch each side), or cut into a larger brunoise of 1/4 inch dice, or cut into larger and thicker cubes based on jardinière.
To break food into small thin pieces, usually by using a fork.
To reduce food into tiny particles using a grinder or a food processor.
To break food into small pieces. A rolling pin, mortar and pestle, blender, or food processor can be used in crushing food.
To crush into a smooth, evenly textured mixture.
To mash or grind food until completely smooth, usually in a food processor, blender, sieve, or food mill.
To use scissors to cut an object into pieces, to remove sections, or to make slits or holes in a product.

Proper measurement of ingredients is essential to having a successful food product. Too much or too little of certain elements, such as salt, baking soda, baking powder, and other hot or spicy ingredients, can affect the texture or taste of the food. There are different measuring methods and measuring equipment used for liquids, dry ingredients, and fats.

terms.term: How to Measure Liquid Ingredients Using a Measuring Cup
terms.definition: Use a liquid measuring cup for accurately measuring thin liquids such as milk, juice, and oil. Put the cup on a flat surface to get an accurate measurement, then pour the liquid in until it reaches the correct measurement line. Use the measurement line, leaning down until reaching eye-level on the measuring cup.

terms.term: How to Measure Liquid Ingredients Using a Spoon
terms.definition: Use a measuring spoon for a small quantity of liquid — use a measuring spoon if measuring less than a quarter cup of a thin liquid. To catch the excess liquid, hold the spoon over a separate bowl and gently pour in the liquid until the spoon is full.

terms.term: How to Measure a Small Amount of Liquid
terms.definition: Use a syringe to measure a small amount of liquid. This tool can also give an accurate result of measurement.
Use a measuring spoon or measuring cup to measure dry ingredients.

The most common way of measuring dry ingredients. It requires dipping the measuring cup into the dry ingredient with the cup overflowing, then taking the back of a knife or a flat spoon handle and sweeping the excess across and off of the measuring cup.
Uses a spoon to fill up the measuring cup with dry ingredients before sweeping off the overflow.
Technically defined as a small fraction of a teaspoon. It often refers to liquids, such as a quick shake of hot sauce or soy sauce.

Technically defined as a small fraction of a teaspoon. It represents the amount that can be held between the thumb and forefinger (e.g., salt, spices) — a way of measuring smaller quantities using the thumb and index finger.

A technique where two or more ingredients are combined and mixed. All terms, such as mix, combine, and blend, refer to mixing. Mixing tools and techniques are used to blend foods in a variety of ways and achieve an array of textures; different tools and appliances are used, including spoons, forks, blenders, and food processors.
Also known as the "sugar shortening" method. The sugar and shortening fat are blended first, then creamed by continued mixing.
To rapidly stir a batter to incorporate the ingredients along with air thoroughly.
A mixing method used to incorporate butter or shortening into dry flour. A pastry blender or a pastry cutter (also called a dough cutter) is used.

To mix the ingredients of a food dish, such as salads and pasta, by lifting and dropping the ingredients/mixture. The food is turned over and mixed, enabling sauces and food items to be seasoned with the flavors of each item.
To mix a substance in a circular pattern using a spoon, spatula, or other similar utensils.
The process of beating ingredients vigorously to incorporate air, making the ingredient frothy.

Combining two mixtures of different thicknesses and weights into one smooth mixture. This is accomplished by a specific technique of using a spoon to lift the two mixtures together, turning them over, so they combine.

Even the most nutritious or beautifully presented meal cannot be truly enjoyed or appreciated by the people eating it if it does not taste good. Seasonings and flavorings are added to foods to enhance their flavor.
Considered the second most frequently used seasoning additive — the first is sugar — although it was introduced as a preservative.
Just behind salt in popularity as a seasoning. Pepper is added most frequently to meats, soups, sauces, and salads.

The aromatic, green leafy parts of non-woody plants. Herbs are well known for their seasoning capabilities in food preparation. The best-known seasoning herbs include basil, sage, thyme, oregano, bay leaves, cilantro, dill, marjoram, mint, parsley, tarragon, rosemary, and savory. For the best flavor and texture, fresh herbs are generally preferred over dried.
Derived from other dried plant parts like roots, bark, seeds, or berries. Some examples include allspice, saffron, cinnamon, mustard, sesame seeds, ginger, and turmeric.

A process of soaking food in a seasoned liquid. Acids (such as vinegar, lemon juice, or wine) and enzymes (such as pineapple, papaya, or ginger) are popularly used, as they help enhance flavors and tenderize the food during marination.
In a marinade, fats such as olive oil, canola oil, coconut milk, full-fat yogurt, or other vegetable oil help preserve the food's moisture.
In a marinade, be cautious when using acid — strong acids make the meat tough. Strong acids can be used in marinades if they are in small quantities or if the meat is marinated only for a few hours.

In a marinade, garlic, onion, salt, chili, peppers, sugars, and aromatics are some of the seasonings that release flavors and add life to the marinade. Whole spices release flavors more slowly, so they are more suitable for long marination.
A high concentration solution of salt in water. The salt solution dissolves the protein in muscle, and the salt and protein reduce moisture loss during cooking, making the food tender and juicy.

sets.name: Definition of Cooking Terms
sets.description: Fundamental culinary terms: cooking processes, technical terms, and French cooking terminology used in kitchen operations.

terms.definition: Cooked so it's still tough when bitten, often referring to pasta.

A container holding hot water into which a pan is placed for slow cooking, otherwise known as a "water bath" or "double boiler". A roasting pan or baking dish partially filled with water to allow food to cook more slowly and be protected from direct high heat. Used for custards and terrines.
To cook foods by surrounding them with hot, dry air. Similar to roast, but this term usually applies to breads, pastries, vegetables, and fish.

(1) To cook with dry heat created by the burning of hardwood or by the hot coals of this wood. (2) Loosely, to cook over hot coals, such as on a grill or spit, often with a seasoned marinade or basting sauce.
To mix ingredients rapidly to incorporate air.

To cook an item partially and very briefly in boiling water or in hot fat. Usually a pre-preparation technique, as to loosen peels of vegetables, fruits, and nuts, to partially cook french fries or other foods before service, to prepare for freezing, or to remove undesirable flavors.
To mix ingredients until smooth.
To cook in water or other liquid that is bubbling rapidly, about 212°F (100°C) at sea level and at normal pressure.
To cook certain vegetables slowly in a small amount of liquid without preliminary browning.

To cook food slowly in a small amount of liquid in a covered pot; a combination-cooking method that first sears the food at high temperature, then finishes it in a covered pot at low temperature while sitting in some amount of liquid.
To cook with radiant heat from above.
To cook submerged in hot fat.
To pour juices or melted fat over meat or other food while cooking to keep it moist.
A thick, creamy soup, with a base of strained broth of shellfish or game.
The process of soaking meat in heavily salted water before cooking, similar to marination.
To cut food into small, irregular pieces.
Shredded or finely cut vegetables and herbs, usually used as a garnish for soup.
A type of clear soup made from richly flavored stock that has been clarified, a process of using egg whites to remove fat.
To mix until smooth and fluffy (e.g., butter and sugar).
To swirl a liquid in a sauté pan, roast pan, or other pan to dissolve cooked particles of food remaining on the bottom.
To cut food into small, uniform cubes.
Methods in which heat is conducted to foods without the use of moisture.
To coat wet or moist foods with a dry ingredient before cooking to provide an even coating.
To put oil, vinegar, salt, or other toppings on a salad or other food.
A boneless piece of meat, poultry, or fish; the French version, spelled as "filet," is also used when referencing a cut of beef that is boneless, such as filet mignon.
The process of adding alcohol such as brandy, cognac, or rum to a hot pan to create a burst of flames.
To cook food in hot oil or fat.
The process of creating a shiny, translucent coating on food, often using a sauce or other liquid, to enhance flavor and appearance.
To cook food over direct heat, usually on a rack.
The process of extracting chemical compounds or flavors from a vegetable in water, oil, or alcohol, by allowing the material to remain suspended in the liquid over time, also known as steeping.
The process of inserting strips of fat into a piece of meat that doesn't have as much fat, to melt and keep the meat from drying out.
A binding agent of cream and egg yolks used to thicken soups or sauces.
To crush food until smooth.
The process of soaking foods in seasoned and acidic liquid before cooking for hours or days, adding flavor to the food.
To finely divide food into uniform pieces smaller than diced or chopped foods, prepared using a chef's knife or food processor.
The preparation of ingredients, such as dicing onions or measuring spices, before starting cooking.
The base sauce used to make other variations of the original sauce.
The process of adding foods to boiling waters, cooking until they are softened, then removing before they are fully cooked, usually to partially cook an item which will then be cooked another way.
The process of not fully cooking food, so that it can be finished or reheated later.
To cook food gently in liquid below boiling point.
To mash or blend until smooth.
To cook the fat out of something, such as bacon.
To cook food using dry heat, usually in an oven.
To cook food quickly over relatively high heat, literally meaning "to jump" as the food does when placed in a hot pan.
To heat a liquid so it's right about to reach the boiling point, where bubbles start to appear around the edges.
A technique used in grilling, baking, or sautéing in which the surface of the food is cooked at high temperature until a crust forms.
To remove foam or fat from liquid surface.

A cooking method that involves exposing food, typically meat, poultry, or fish, to smoke from burning or smoldering material, most often wood, to impart flavor, color, and potentially preserve the food.
To cook in liquid just below boiling point.
To cook food using the vapor from boiling water.
Gently heating vegetables in a little oil, with frequent stirring and turning to ensure emitted liquid will evaporate; usually results in tender, or in some cases such as onions', translucent pieces.
Raising the temperature of a cold or room-temperature ingredient by slowly adding hot or boiling liquid, often referring to eggs.
To make meat softer by pounding or marinating.
To tie meat or poultry, such as turkey with a string, woven through the bird parts by using a needle, in order to create a more compact shape before cooking.
A type of sauce in which a light stock, such as chicken or fish, is thickened with a flour that is cooked and then allowed to turn light brown; made from butter, flour, cream and stock.
To beat food with a mixer to incorporate air and produce volume, often used to create heavy cream, salad dressings, or sauces.
A cooking utensil used to blend ingredients in a process such as whipping.
Butter and flour mixed together in equal parts and used to thicken liquids.
Broth or stock.
A mixture of fresh herbs tied together with string and used to flavor stews, soups etc. It refers to a mix of parsley, bay leaf, thyme (and sometimes celery stalk). It is removed before serving.
Vegetables cut into very small diced pieces.
An appetizer consisting of a small bread or biscuit base covered with flavored topping.
The term used to refer to the actual main course.
Dessert or sweet.
First course or appetizer.
To cut food into thin, matchstick-like strips.
Small diced mixed vegetables, usually containing at least one root vegetable. Sometimes also means a mixture of fruit, like fruit salad.
A mixture of braising vegetables.
Translates to "in paper" or "in parchment". A French cooking term that refers to a method of cooking where food is enclosed in a folded packet of parchment paper or foil and then baked.
A sweet or pastry. Also refers to cake shop.
Melted butter which is added with flour. It is usually used as a thickener for sauces or soups.

sets.name: Food Preparation Tools and Equipment
sets.description: Cookware, cooking and processing equipment, measuring devices, knives, hand tools, and small equipment, with their uses and functions.

terms.definition: Deep, round containers used for cooking food, usually on the stovetop. Common uses: boiling, simmering, making soups, stews, or pasta.
Shallow cookware with flat bottoms, used for frying, sautéing, or baking. Common uses: frying eggs, cooking meat, sautéing vegetables.
Containers used to shape food as it cools or sets. Common uses: making cakes, gelatin desserts, chocolates, or puddings. They come in many shapes and sizes, made of metal, silicone, or plastic.
A large, deep, straight-sided pot for preparing stocks and simmering large quantities of liquids. Sizes: 8–200 quarts (liters).
A round pot of medium depth. Similar to a stockpot but shallower, making stirring or mixing easier. Used for soups, sauces, and other liquids. Sizes: 6–60 quarts (liters).
A round, broad, shallow, heavy-duty pot with straight sides. Also called a rondeau. Used for browning, braising, and stewing meats. Sizes: 11–30 quarts (liters).

Similar to a small, shallow, light saucepot, but with one long handle instead of two loop handles. May have straight or slanted sides. Used for general range top cooking. Sizes: 1 1/2–15 quarts (liters).
A straight-sided sauté pan. Similar to a shallow, straight-sided saucepan, but heavier. Used for browning, sautéing, and frying; its wide surface allows quick reduction of sauces and liquids.

A slope-sided sauté pan. Used for general sautéing and frying of meats, fish, vegetables, and eggs. The sloping sides allow the cook to flip and toss items without using a spatula, and they make it easier to get at the food when a spatula is used. Sizes: 6–14 inches (160–360 mm) top diameter.
Very heavy, thick-bottomed fry pan. Used for pan-frying when steady, even heat is desired.

A pot with two sections. The lower section, similar to a stockpot, holds boiling water. The upper section holds foods that must be cooked at low temperatures and cannot be cooked over direct heat. Size of top section: 4–36 quarts (liters).
A shallow, rectangular pan (1 inch/25 mm deep) for baking cakes, rolls, and cookies, and for baking or broiling certain meats and fish. Sizes: full pan, 18 × 26 inches (46 × 66 cm).
A rectangular pan about 2 inches (50 mm) deep. Used for general baking. Available in a variety of sizes.
A large rectangular pan, deeper and heavier than a bake pan. Used for roasting meats and poultry.

Also called counter pan, steam table pan, or service pan. A rectangular pan, usually made of stainless steel. Designed to hold foods in service counters. Also used for baking, steaming, and subsequent serving, and for storage. Standard size: 12 × 20 inches.

A round-bottomed steel pan with two loop handles. Used for stir-frying, especially in Chinese cuisine. These are best used with special burner units that have a high heat output and a broad ring-shaped support that holds it steady during cooking.
Containers placed over or inside hot water to gently heat or keep food warm without direct heat. They are commonly used for sauces, soups, and delicate foods to prevent burning or overheating.

The range is still the most important piece of cooking equipment in the kitchen. These are the top surface of a stove where burners are located, used for cooking food in pots and pans over direct heat.
Also called the commercial range. The most commonly used in professional kitchens. It provides strong heat, instant control, and is ideal for sautéing, boiling, and general cooking.
Uses coils or a smooth glass surface. It is easy to operate and clean but heats and cools more slowly than gas.
Popular in modern kitchens. It heats quickly, is energy-efficient, and safer because it only heats the cookware, not the surface.

Also called heavy-duty electric. Known for durability and consistent heat. Often used in kitchens that need long cooking hours, though it heats slower. Its disadvantage is that only iron or steel pots can be used.
Also called the flat top range. A large flat surface with a central heat source. Chefs can cook multiple dishes at different temperatures by moving pots around.
Enclosed spaces in which food is heated, usually by hot air or, in some newer kinds, by microwaves or infrared radiation.

The traditional type found in most kitchens. It operates simply by heating air in an enclosed space, using top and bottom heating elements to cook food without a fan, so heat moves naturally inside. The most common are part of the range unit, although separate units or those forming part of a broiler unit are also available.

Contains fans that circulate the air and distribute the heat rapidly throughout the interior. Because of the forced air, foods cook more quickly at lower temperatures. Also, shelves can be placed closer together than in conventional ovens without blocking the heat flow.

Kitchen equipment that cooks food using very high heat from above; sometimes called overhead to avoid confusing them with grills. Commonly used for grilling, browning, and finishing dishes like steaks, casseroles, and melted toppings.

Used for the same cooking operations as broilers, except the heat source is below the grid that holds the food rather than above it. Many people like foods cooked this way because of their charcoal taste, which is created by smoke from meat fats that drip into the heat source.

Small broilers used primarily for browning or glazing the tops of some items. A type of overhead broiler mounted on the wall or above a range. Used for quick finishing, melting cheese, glazing, and browning dishes before serving.
Flat smooth, heated surfaces on which food is cooked directly. Pancakes, French toast, hamburgers and other meats, eggs, and potato items are the foods most frequently cooked on these.

Cook meats and other foods by turning them slowly in front of electric- or gas-powered heating elements. Although especially suitable for chicken and other poultry, they can be used to cook any meat or other food that can be held on a spit or in any of various attachments or accessories. Both enclosed (oven like) and open or unclosed units are available.
Vertical ones are important and versatile tools for many kinds of food mixing and processing jobs, both in the bakeshop and in the kitchen.
A flat blade used for general mixing.
Also called the dough hook. Used for mixing and kneading yeast doughs.
Also called the rotation chopper and familiarly known as the buffalo chopper. A common piece of equipment used for general food chopping.

terms.term: The 3 Ways Measurements are Determined in a Professional Kitchen

terms.definition: Portion ones are used for measuring ingredients as well as for portioning products for service. Traditional portion ones are spring-operated and usually have a dial to indicate weight.
Those used for liquids have lips for easy pouring. Sizes are pints, quarts, half-gallons, and gallons. Each size is marked off into fourths by ridges on the sides.
Available in 1-, 1/2-, 1/3-, and 1/4-cup sizes. They can be used for both liquid and dry measures.
Used for measuring very small volumes: 1 tablespoon, 1 teaspoon, 1/2 teaspoon, and 1/4 teaspoon. They are used most often for spices and seasonings.
Measure temperature. There are many kinds for many purposes.
Indicates internal temperature of meats. It is inserted before cooking and left in the product during cooking.
Tests temperatures of frying fats.
Tests temperatures of sugar syrups.
One of the chef's most important hand tools.
The most widely available material for knife blades.
Used for knife handles. Easy to maintain, but they can become a hazard if the material is gouged, cracked, or melted.
Most frequently used knife in the kitchen, for general-purpose chopping, slicing, dicing, and so on. The blade is wide at the heel and tapers to a point.
Also called the Japanese cook's knife. A wide-bladed knife that is often used as a substitute for the traditional chef's knife. Blades are usually 5 inches (13 cm) or 7 inches (18 cm) long.
Also called the salad knife. A narrow, pointed knife 6–8 inches (160–200 mm) long. Used mostly for pantry work.
A small, pointed blade 2–4 inches (50–100 mm) long. Used for trimming and paring vegetables and fruits.
A thin, pointed blade about 6 inches (160 mm) long. Used for boning raw meats and poultry. Stiff blades are used for heavier work. Flexible blades are used for lighter work and for filleting fish.
A long, slender, flexible blade up to 14 inches (360 mm) long. Used for carving and slicing cooked meats.
Like a slicer, but with a serrated edge. Used for cutting breads, cakes, and similar items.
A heavy, broad, slightly curved blade. Used for cutting, sectioning, and trimming raw meats in the butcher shop.
Also called the steak knife. A curved, pointed blade. Used for accurate cutting of steaks.
A heavy, broad blade. Used for cutting through bones.
A short tool with a slotted, swiveling blade. Used for peeling vegetables and fruits.
Not a knife, but an essential part of the knife kit. Used for truing and maintaining knife edges.

An important partner to the knife. Hardwood ones are favored by many chefs. Hard rubber or plastic ones are thought to be more sanitary, but there is some evidence that bacteria actually survive longer on plastic and rubber than on wood. They must be kept very clean and sanitized regularly. Color-coded composite ones are designed to help reduce cross-contamination, as each color is used for a different category of food.
A heavy, two-pronged fork with a long handle. Used for lifting and turning meats and other items. Must be strong enough to hold heavy loads.
Also called the palette knife. A long, flexible blade with a rounded end. Used mostly for spreading icing on cakes and for mixing and bowl scraping.

A broad blade, bent to keep the hand off hot surfaces. Used for turning and lifting eggs, pancakes, and meats on griddles, grills, sheet pans, and so on. Also used as a scraper to clean benches and griddles.
Also called the scraper. A broad, flexible rubber or plastic tip on a long handle. Used to scrape bowls and pans. Also used for folding in egg foams and whipped cream.
A wedge-shaped offset spatula. Used for lifting pie wedges from pan.
Also called the dough knife. A broad, stiff piece of metal with a wooden handle on one edge. Used to cut pieces of dough and to scrape workbenches.
Also called the wheel knife. A round, rotating blade on a handle. Used for cutting rolled out doughs and pastry and baked pizza.
A perforated disk, slightly cupped, on a long handle. Used for skimming froth from liquids and for removing solid pieces from soups, stocks, and other liquids.
Spring-type or scissors-type tools used to pick up and handle foods.
A mixing attachment used for such tasks as beating cream and eggs and making mayonnaise. Loops of stainless-steel wire fastened to a handle.
Straight, stiff, and have relatively few wires. Used for general mixing, stirring, and beating, especially heavy liquids.
Also called piano-wire whips. They have many flexible wires. Used for whipping eggs, cream, and hollandaise, and for mixing thinner liquids.
A cone-shaped strainer. Used for straining stocks, soups, sauces, and other liquids. Pointed shape allows the cook to drain liquids through a relatively small opening.
A round-bottomed, cup-shaped tool made of screen type mesh or perforated metal. Used for straining pasta, vegetables, and so on.
Also called the tamis. A screen-type mesh supported in a round metal frame. Used for sifting flour and other dry ingredients and for puréeing soft foods.
A large, perforated bowl made of stainless steel or aluminum. Used to drain washed or cooked vegetables, salad greens, pasta, and other foods.
A tool with a hand-turned blade that forces foods through a perforated disk. Interchangeable disks produce varying degrees of coarseness or fineness. Used for puréeing foods.
A four-sided metal box with grids of varying sizes. Used for shredding and grating vegetables, cheese, citrus rinds, and other foods.
A small hand tool used for removing the colored part of citrus peels in thin strips.

A round-bottomed bowl. Used for mixing, whipping, and producing hollandaise, mayonnaise, whipped cream, and egg white foams. Round construction enables whip to reach all areas. Available in many sizes.

A manual slicing implement consisting of blades fitted in a flat metal or wood framework. A traditional one has a flat blade and a serrated blade. Additional blades can be used in combination with the flat blade to cut julienne and bâtonnet.

Cone-shaped cloths or plastic bags with an open end that can be fitted with metal tubes or tips of various shapes and sizes. Used for shaping and decorating with items such as cake icing, whipped cream, potatoes, and soft dough. Disposable plastic ones are the most sanitary.
Used to brush items with egg wash, glaze, etc.

A type of large, deep-bowled serving spoon with a long handle, designed for scooping and serving liquids like soups, stews, sauces, or gravy. Primarily a kitchen tool, they are often crafted from stainless steel, plastic, or wood.

sets.name: History of Culinary Arts
sets.description: The historical development of culinary arts, the three classes of French cuisine, the culinary timeline, and the famous French chefs and their contributions.

terms.definition: The city where the first cooking school was traced back to in the 1800s, teaching the art of American cooking along with preparing the students to pass on their knowledge to others.
In 1946, he held regular cooking classes on the art of American cooking.
She introduced French cuisine to Americans in the 1960's.

Translates to "high cuisine" and refers to a shift in French cooking from an emphasis on abundance and quantity to an emphasis on moderation and quality. Marie Antoine Careme is often credited with leading this charge in the 1800s. He taught French cooking as a sophisticated art form that required technique and precision, and his recipe manuals made French cuisine more accessible.

French cooking continued to evolve and in the 1900s, this style was born. It was defined by the use of high-quality, fresh ingredients; lighter meals; and simpler yet breathtaking presentations. Modern French cooking draws inspiration from the many cooking concepts French chefs have developed and presented over centuries.
Its rich tapestry is as ancient as the French regions themselves. Historically, local cooking was shaped by geographical conditions, available resources, and neighboring influences.
In 1500, these were established to dictate and monopolize food preparation.

A Parisian who in 1765 opened the first free-standing restaurant in Paris. He was challenged in court by the guild of stew makers because he served sheep's feet in a cream sauce; the guild claimed he replicated the dish, but he won the case by claiming that he didn't stew the feet in the sauce but served it with the sauce. Because of what happened, he unintentionally changed the development of food-service history.
The name Boulanger gave his 1765 Parisian establishment, from a word literally meaning "fortifying" or to bring life back.
1789-1799. The social structure in France changed. The aristocracy guilds and their monopolies were abolished. The growing restaurant industry emerged.

1783-1833. Also known as "The King of Chefs and the Chef of Kings" and the First Celebrity Chef. His goal was to achieve "lightness, grace, order and perspicuity in the preparation and presentation of food." As a saucier, he standardized the use of roux and devised a system to classify sauces; as a culinary professional, he designed kitchen tools, equipment and uniforms. An illustrious French chef, the most famous author and culinary artist during the 1800s and one of the most prolific food writers of the 19th century, he codified the four original Mother Sauces in the early 1800s.

1846-1935. Known as the "Father of Modern French Culinary Arts," the "king of the Kitchen" and the "father of modern French cuisine." He simplified food preparation and dining and conceptualized the so-called kitchen brigade system used in large kitchens today. He classified the five families of sauces. An author of par excellence, he wrote Le livres de menus, Ma Cuisine, and Le Guide Culinaire, which is still in use today. He recognized garde manger as a specialized type of work significantly different from hot foods cooking, and physically separated the garde manger station from the hot line.
1886-1899. The "First renowned chef of an American restaurant," Delmonico in New York City. His goal was to serve fresh seasonal and locally grown produce.
1897-1955. He refined and modernized classical cuisine and laid the groundwork for Nouvelle Cuisine.

1920-2009. The "Father of modern French Pastry." He began a culinary school named Le Ecole Norte. He developed innovations in modern pastries such as Bavarians, Charlottes and Mousses, and mastered the techniques in freezing baked products.

Founder of modern French cuisine. He is credited as the first to use roux as a thickener, and to refine the technique of dough lamination to make an early form of puff pastry. He lightened and simplified European cooking and popularized fresh vegetables and herbs.

sets.name: Kitchen Conversion
sets.description: What kitchen conversion is and why it matters, the types of kitchen measurements, common measurement abbreviations, and key volume, weight, and temperature equivalents.

terms.definition: Refers to the process of changing one unit of measurement to another when preparing food or following recipes in the kitchen. It is essential for accuracy in cooking and baking, especially when recipes use different systems of measurement.

terms.term: The 6 Reasons Kitchen Conversions Are Important

terms.definition: Helps chefs follow recipes exactly for consistent quality.
Same taste, look, and portion every time for every customer.
Quick conversions help kitchen staff work faster.
Right measurements mean less ingredient waste.
Easy to adjust recipes for big batches or events.
Accurate portions help control food costs and avoid overuse.
Measured in milliliters (ml), liters (L), cups, tablespoons (tbsp), teaspoons (tsp), fluid ounces (fl oz), pints, quarts, and gallons; used for liquid ingredients.
Measured in grams (g), kilograms (kg), ounces (oz), and pounds (lbs); used for solid ingredients.
Measured in Celsius (°C) and Fahrenheit (°F).
Measured in inches and centimeters; used for cutting and portioning.
Abbreviated tsp. A volume unit used for small amounts of ingredients, such as salt and spices.
Abbreviated tbsp. A volume unit larger than a teaspoon; commonly used in cooking and baking.
Abbreviated c. A volume unit used for both liquid and dry ingredients.
Abbreviated oz. Used for weight (solid ingredients) or as fluid ounces (liquid ingredients).
Abbreviated fl oz. A volume unit used specifically for liquid measurements.
Abbreviated lb. A weight unit equal to 16 ounces; used for heavier ingredients.
Abbreviated g. A metric weight unit used for measuring light ingredients.
Abbreviated kg. A metric weight unit equal to 1000 grams; used for bulk ingredients.
Abbreviated mL. A metric volume unit used for measuring liquids, including bulk ingredients.
Abbreviated L. A metric volume unit equal to 1000 milliliters; used for larger liquids.
Abbreviated pt. A volume unit common in liquid measurements, equal to 2 cups.
Abbreviated qt. A volume unit equal to 4 cups.
Abbreviated gal. A volume unit equal to 16 cups; used for large quantities.
Abbreviated °C. The metric unit for temperature in cooking.
Abbreviated °F. The standard unit for temperature, used in ovens.

3 teaspoons = 1 tablespoon = 1/16 cup. 6 teaspoons = 2 tablespoons = 1/8 cup. 12 teaspoons = 4 tablespoons = 1/4 cup. 24 teaspoons = 8 tablespoons = 1/2 cup. 36 teaspoons = 12 tablespoons = 3/4 cup. 48 teaspoons = 16 tablespoons = 1 cup.
1 cup = 8 fluid ounces = 16 tablespoons = 48 teaspoons = 1/2 pint = 1/4 quart = 1/16 gallon.
1 gallon = 4 quarts = 8 pints = 16 cups = 128 ounces = 3.8 liters. 1 quart = 2 pints = 4 cups = 32 ounces = 0.95 liters. 1 pint = 2 cups = 16 ounces = 480 mL.
Equal to 1,000 g/ml, 4.22 cups, and 2.2 lbs.
By volume, 1/2 cup or 125 mL. By weight, 1/4 lb (4 oz) or 115 g.

sets.name: Meat
sets.description: What meat is, beef and pork classifications, the structure of meat, beef and pork retail cuts and their Filipino names, variety meats, and processed meats.

terms.definition: One of the most important ingredients in culinary, valued for its rich flavor, nutritional content, and versatility in cooking. It is a primary source of protein, vitamins, and minerals essential for body growth and development. In the kitchen, understanding meat is crucial because its quality, cut, and preparation greatly affect the outcome of a dish. In the Philippines, meat from herbivores such as beef cattle, sheep, goat, and swine serves as the most common source of meat. Meat is generally defined as the muscles of animals, but in a broader sense, it also covers the organs and glands obtained from the animal. Although the word meat includes the flesh of poultry and fish, these are each covered separately.
Originates from cattle that are classified according to age and gender.
Male cattle that are castrated while young so that they will gain weight quickly.
Older, uncastrated male cattle that provide stag meat. Consumers often do not see the tougher meat from bulls, as they are usually used for breeding and then later for processed meats and pet foods.
Female cattle that have not borne a calf; also used for meat.
Female cattle that have borne calves. The meat from cows is less desirable than that from steers or heifers.
Cattle 3 to 8 months old — too old for veal and too young for beef. If they go to market between 8 and 12 months, their meat is referred to as baby beef.

Young swine of either gender (male or female) slaughtered between the first 5 1/2 and 7 months of age are the most common source of pork. About 1/3 of all pork is sold fresh, and the rest is made into ham, sausage, luncheon meats, and bacon.
Technically, swine less than 4 months old.
Technically, swine older than 4 months.
Meats are composed of a combination of water, muscle, connective tissue, adipose (fatty) tissue, and often bone.
Most of the proteins in meat are found in the muscles. Leaner cuts of muscle tissue yield lesser calories.

Part of ligaments and tendons; it acts as the "glue" that holds muscle cells together. The most abundant protein in connective tissue is collagen and elastin. Collagen is tough and fibrous, but converts to a gel when exposed to moist heat.
Simply, fat, which serves as insulation under the skin and as padding for internal organs.
Fat found within muscles, also called intramuscular fat, deposited in the muscle and seen as little white streaks or drops. Marbling contributes to the flavor and juiciness of meat.
In meat, bones are used as landmarks for identifying the various meat cuts from a carcass. Older animals have whiter bones; younger animals have reddish bones.
A soft, fatty material in the center of most large bones. Marrow is a valued food in many countries, as it provides much of the flavor in stocks and soups.

Rib, short loin, and sirloin wholesale cuts lie along the back of the animal and are usually the most tender and expensive cuts of beef. Rib roasts are the most tender roasts, and tenderloin is the most tender steak. The least tender wholesale cuts are flank, short plate, brisket, and foreshank.
The small end of the tenderloin.

terms.term: The 9 Filipino Names for Beef Cuts

terms.definition: The Filipino butchery term for the beef shank and bone marrow cut.
The Filipino butchery term for the beef chuck rib cut.
The Filipino butchery term for the beef blade clod cut.
The Filipino butchery term for beef short ribs.
The Filipino butchery term for the beef sirloin cut.
The Filipino butchery term for beef tenderloin.
The Filipino butchery term for the tender chuck cut of beef.
The Filipino butchery term for beef brisket.
The Filipino butchery term for the beef flank steak cut.

Pork is usually tender regardless of the cut. Wholesale loin and spare rib cuts of pork are much longer than beef and lamb, because the rib and sirloin are not separated in the carcass. The leg is the largest primal cut in pork; because pork is slaughtered at a young age, pork legs are very tender for roasting.

terms.term: The 2 Wholesale Cuts That Provide Most Fresh Pork Retail Cuts

terms.definition: As a wholesale pork cut, it provides pork loin chop or roast, Canadian-style bacon, and pork loin tenderloin.
As a wholesale pork cut, it provides spare ribs, bacon, and rib bacon.

terms.term: The 17 Parts of a Pork Carcass
The 5 Filipino Names for Pork Cuts

terms.definition: The Filipino butchery term for the pork shoulder cut.
The Filipino butchery term for the pork loin cut.
The Filipino butchery term for the pork ham cut.
The Filipino butchery term for pork belly.
The Filipino butchery term for the pork hock.

Also known as organ and offal. They can be either organ meats or muscle meats. Organ meats are very soft, extremely tender, and easily cooked — examples are liver, kidneys, and brains. Muscle meats require long and slow cooking, as they are heavily exercised muscles and are quite tough — examples include tongue and heart.

About one-third of all meat is processed by different methods such as curing, smoking, canning, and drying, meaning it has changed from its original "fresh" cut. Examples include ham, sausages, and bacon.
Cured pork. According to USDA (United States Department of Agriculture) standards, only meat from the hind leg of a hog can be labeled ham.
Cured and smoked meat from the side of a hog.
Meat that has been finely chopped or ground and blended with various ingredients, seasonings, and spices. It is then stuffed into casings or skins.

sets.name: Sanitation and Food Safety in Culinary Operations
sets.description: Food safety, R.A. 10611, the three major types of food hazards, food handlers, and the ten principles of safe food handling and hygiene.

terms.definition: Refers to handling, preparing and storing food in a way to best reduce the risk of individuals becoming sick from foodborne illnesses. It is the protection of consumer health and well-being by safeguarding food from anything that can cause harm.

An act to strengthen the food safety regulatory system in the country to protect consumer health and facilitate market access of local foods and food products, and for other purposes; otherwise known as the "Food Safety Act of 2013".

terms.term: The 3 Major Types of Hazards in Food Safety

terms.definition: Foodborne organisms such as bacteria, molds, viruses, and parasites. Their seriousness varies greatly. It is difficult to avoid microorganisms because they are everywhere. However, most are inactivated or killed by adequate cooking and/or their numbers are kept to a minimum by sufficient cooling.

Any substances hazardous to health. These can come from plants (herbs, fruit pits, and mushrooms), animals (fish), or those used in agriculture or industry that may end up in food unintentionally. Both fish and shellfish may harbor toxins causing foodborne illness. Not all fishes and plants are consumable, such as pufferfish and amanita species of mushrooms.
During this time there is an increased chance that seafood products are poisonous, which is why people are very careful in buying seafood products.

Items in food and beverages that can harm the consumer's health, including glass (the most common), bone, metal, wood, stones, false fingernails, toothpicks, watches, jewelry, insects, staples from food boxes, and many other foreign items that have been known to find their way into the food supply.
Those whose work involves food; anyone who works in a food business where food is processed, prepared, stored, distributed, or exposed for sale. Their role is ensuring the food produced is safe.

terms.term: The 10 Principles of Safe Food Handling & Hygiene
answers: Cooking by appropriate temperature and procedures

sets.name: The Kitchen Organization and Layout
sets.description: The kitchen and its areas and sub-sections, the work triangle and layout shapes, and the classical kitchen brigade positions.

terms.definition: The heart of food operations where preparation, cooking, and storage happen. A room or part of a room used for cooking and food preparation, with a stove, sink with hot and cold running water, a refrigerator and cabinets arranged there. Its main function is cooking or preparing food but it may also be used for dining, food storage, entertaining, and dishwashing.

terms.term: The 4 Other Functions of the Kitchen
answers: Production and presentation of quality foods using a tested recipe
Preparation of menus and standard recipe
Dispatching of food to foodcounters and dining areas

terms.definition: Where ingredients are washed, cut, and made ready for cooking.
Where food is actually cooked using different methods such as boiling, frying, or baking.
Where food is arranged and prepared for serving.
Where ingredients and supplies are kept (dry, cold, and frozen).
Where used tools, utensils, and equipment are cleaned and sanitized.
Part of the kitchen where dishes like salads and cold cuts, etc. are prepared. It is also in this area that cold and fruit platters as well as garnishes are prepared.
Part of the kitchen that handles the preparation of all hot items like stocks, soup, sauces and main dishes.
The area where meat, chicken and seafood items are portion cut in accordance with standard sizes and weights that are indicated in standard recipes.
The section responsible for preparing all baked goods, desserts, and other sweet treats. This area typically includes a variety of specialized equipment and tasks, such as baking and decorating.

One of the most basic layout principles. An imaginary line drawn from each of the three primary work stations in the kitchen — the food storage, preparation/cooking, and clean-up stations. By drawing these lines, you can assess the distance required to move to and from each area and thus determine how well the traffic will flow. To help avoid traffic flow problems, it should have a perimeter that measures less than 26 feet.

terms.term: The 3 Primary Kitchen Work Stations Constituting the Work Triangle

terms.definition: The refrigerator and pantry are the major items here. Cabinetries like lazy Susan or swing-out pantry units add function and convenience. Options like wine racks, spice racks, and roll-out trays help to organize your groceries.
The range, oven, microwave, and smaller appliances are found in this area. Counter space is important in this section.

Everyone's least favorite activity is one of the kitchen's most important. This area is home to the sink, waste disposal, and dishwasher. Cabinetry for this station is designed to organize the trash bin cabinet and roll-out tray baskets for storage convenience.

Named for the shape it resembles, this kitchen is popular in large and small homes alike. Perfect for families who use their kitchens a great deal; provides plenty of counter space; efficient work triangle.

This kitchen shape is one of the most flexible and most popular, providing a compact triangle. Very flexible layout design; major appliances can be placed in a variety of areas; work areas are close to each other.

Extremely popular in homes today and most often seen in L-Shaped kitchens. It can not only keep work areas traffic-free, but also create a wealth of extra counter and storage space. It can be an indispensable food preparation station or act as a butcher block area.

Built very much like the U-Shaped with the addition of an elongated partial wall, it offers a great deal of space. Plenty of counter and cabinet space; multiple cooks can function well in this layout; can convert one cabinet leg into a breakfast bar or entertaining area.

Also called the corridor kitchen. This style makes the most out of a smaller space. Great for smaller kitchens; appliances are close to one another; easy for one cook to maneuver; can easily convert to a U-Shape by closing off one end.

Refers to the structured arrangement of roles and responsibilities of staff, ensuring that each member has a specific duty to maintain efficiency, coordination, and smooth workflow in food preparation.
The most common system used in kitchen organization, developed by Auguste Escoffier.

Is responsible for overall management of kitchen; supervises staff, creates menus and new recipes with the assistance of the restaurant manager, makes purchases of raw food items, trains apprentices, and maintains a sanitary and hygienic environment for the preparation of food.

Sub Chief or Deputy Kitchen Chef. He or she receives orders directly from the Chef de Cuisine for the management of the kitchen. Often serves as the representative when the Chef de Cuisine is not present.
Station Head. He or she is responsible for managing a given station in the kitchen, specializing in preparing particular dishes there.
Assistant Station Chef. Does most of the actual preparation of food in the kitchen.
Junior Cook. Also works in a specific station, but reports directly to the Chef de Partie and takes care of the tools for the station.
Sauté Station Chef. Prepares sauces and warm hors d'oeuvres, completes meat dishes, and in smaller restaurants, may work on fish dishes and prepare sautéed items.
Roast Station Chef. He or she is responsible for the preparation of all roasted food items. Manages a team of cooks that roasts and broils.
Grill Station Chef. Prepares grilled foods instead of the rôtisseur. He or she is responsible for all the grilled foods.
Fish Station Chef. He or she is responsible for the preparation of all fish and seafood dishes.
Fry Station Chef. He or she is responsible for fried meats, seafood and etc. In larger kitchens, prepares fried foods instead of the rôtisseur.
Chicken Station Chef. He or she is responsible for the preparation of all chicken or poultry dishes.
Vegetable Station Chef. Prepares the vegetable dishes and also reports to the entremetier.
Soup Station Chef. Prepares the soups and reports to the entremetier.

terms.term: The 4 Specialized Areas of the Kitchen Brigade

terms.definition: Petit Fours Preparer. In larger restaurants, prepares candies and petits fours instead of the pâtissier.
Frozen and Cold Dessert Preparer. In larger restaurants, prepares frozen and cold desserts instead of the pâtissier. Makes ice carving for presentation.
Cake Designer or Decorator. In larger restaurants, prepares show pieces and specialty cakes instead of the pâtissier.
Baker. In larger restaurants, prepares bread, cakes, and breakfast pastries instead of the pâtissier.
Butcher. Butchers meats, poultry, and sometimes fish; may also be in charge of breading meat and fish items.
Announcer or Expediter. Takes orders from the dining room and distributes them to the various stations; may also be performed by the sous-chef de partie.
Spare Hand or Rounds Man. He or she moves throughout the kitchen, assisting other positions in kitchen.
Literally "Kitchen Boy". In larger restaurants, performs preparatory and "auxiliary" (back-up) work for support.
Apprentice. Students gaining theoretical and practical training in the kitchen.
Dishwasher or Kitchen Porter. Cleans dishes and utensils.
Pot and Pan Washer. Takes care of all the pots and pans instead of the plongeur.

sets.name: Types of Cooking Method
sets.description: The three categories of cooking methods, the moist heat and dry heat techniques, dry heat techniques using fat, and the combination heat techniques of braising and stewing.

terms.definition: Cooking methods are divided into three main categories: dry heat, moist heat, and combination heat, which use conduction, convection, or radiation to change food texture and flavor. Choosing the right method affects nutrition, texture, and flavor.
The process of heating food using liquid other than oil.

A way of cooking food without using water, broth, or steam as the primary heat transfer medium. Instead, it uses direct heat (like from flames, hot air, or hot metal) or indirect heat (like in an oven) to cook the food.
Techniques that combine dry and moist heat, starting with high heat to brown the food and finishing with low, moist heat to tenderize it.

A moist heat cooking technique that cooks food in a liquid, such as water or stocks, that is bubbling rapidly and greatly agitated. The boiling point of water is 100°C (212°F) at sea level. The food can be added and cooked when the liquid reaches its boiling point; no matter how high the heat is on, the liquid temperature will go no higher. Boiling is commonly used in cooking vegetables and starches — the protein of meats is toughened by the high temperatures, while the rapid bubbling breaks up delicate foods.

A moist heat cooking technique that involves cooking food in a liquid heated at 85°C to 93°C (185°F to 200°F). With a lower temperature, simmering makes a gentler process of cooking compared to boiling. The food is cooked slower, creating better control of evaporation and breaking up of delicate foods. This cooking technique is used to lessen the volume of liquid.

A moist heat cooking technique that involves cooking food in a small amount of liquid, enough to cover the food, between 66°C (150°F) and 85°C (185°F). This process is gentler than simmering. Poaching is used to cook delicate food, such as egg and fish, or to cook a variety of meat to remove undesirable flavors and firm the product before final cooking.

A moist heat cooking technique where food is partially and briefly immersed into boiling water. This is the fastest way to change the flavor and enhance the color of the food. Blanching is also used to preserve the nutritional value of the food and remove blood, salt, or impurities from meats and bones. It also helps loosen the skin of vegetables and fruits, which simplifies peeling.

The two steps involved in blanching food in water: immerse the food in boiling water and return the pot to a boil to partially cook it, then remove the blanched food from the liquid and plunge it into ice water to stop the cooking process.

A moist heat cooking technique similar to blanching, where food is partially cooked by immersing it into boiling water; however, it requires a longer cooking time than blanching, and it does not cool the food using cold water or ice after removing it from the boiling water. Poisonous and bad-tasting substances from foods can be removed through parboiling. It is also used to soften vegetables before grilling and roasting them.

A moist heat cooking technique where food is cooked by directly exposing it to hot steam. Food is cooked using an enclosed pot and a steamer basket: the food is put inside a covered steamer basket and placed over the pot filled with a small amount of water. The water from the pot is heated until it reaches the boiling point, and from a closed environment, it creates hot steam that serves as heat to the food.

Works without the presence of any moisture, broth, or water. Instead, it relies on the circulation of hot air or contact with fat to transfer heat to foods. Temperatures of 300 degrees or hotter are used to create browning, a reaction where the amino acids and sugars in food turn brown and create a distinct aroma and flavor.
The reaction that occurs at temperatures of 300 degrees or hotter, where the amino acids and sugars in food turn brown and create a distinct aroma and flavor.

Baking and roasting both use indirect heat to surround foods and cook from all sides. The term roasting is used when cooking meats or vegetables, and baking is used when making bread, rolls, and cakes. Technically, these cooking methods are the same, but baking is usually performed at lower temperatures than roasting.
Can be performed at very low temperatures between 200 degrees and 350 degrees Fahrenheit for tougher cuts of meat, or higher temperatures up to 450 degrees Fahrenheit for more tender cuts.

Works by transferring extremely high heat onto food, usually directed from a radiant located above the food, which cooks on one side at a time. Browning can occur very quickly with this method, sealing juices and flavor inside and leaving a crisp exterior. Because this cooking method is fast, it's helpful to use a timer or check the doneness so foods don't become burnt or overcooked. In commercial kitchens, broiling can be performed with a broiler oven.

The heat should be turned on full. The cooking temperature can be controlled by adjusting the rack nearer or farther from the heat source: thicker food items should be placed farther from the heat source, while thinner items should be placed nearer the heat source, so the inner and outer portions of the food cook at the same rate. The broiler should be preheated, which helps the food product sear quickly and achieve the desired grill marks. Dipping food in oil will avoid it from drying and sticking, though this is not necessary for high-fat foods — be careful about the amount of fat, as too much oil on a hot broiler may cause a fire.
A low-intensity broiler that is used for browning or melting the top of food items before being served.

terms.term: The 3 Dry Heat Cooking Techniques That Use Heat Underneath

terms.definition: Similar to broiling, in that it uses radiant heat to cook foods quickly. Most commonly, grilling equipment will feature an open grate with a heat source located beneath the food. Flipping is required to cook foods on both sides, and grill marks from the hot grate or rack are desirable.

Done on a solid metal surface called a griddle, with a gas or an electric heat source. A small amount of fat is added, depending on the type of food being cooked, to prevent the food from sticking. The temperature is adjustable and much lower (around 177°C/350°F) than on a grill.
Like griddling, except it is done in a sauté pan or skillet instead of a griddle. Fat must be poured off as it accumulates, or the process becomes pan-frying.

terms.term: The 6 Dry Heat Cooking Techniques That Use Fat

terms.definition: A cooking technique that exposes ingredients (typically meat) to a high temperature to create a crisp browning on the outside. This method enhances the flavor of the dish and is often done in a small amount of oil, butter, or fat.

terms.term: Searing Food on a Range Top
terms.definition: Heat the pan and put in a small amount of oil. Place the food when the oil is already hot. Brown the meat on one side, then turn it to brown the other side. Once both sides are browned, place the pan into a hot oven to finish the cooking process.

Place the food into a pan and cook it at 232°C to 242°C (450°F to 475°F) in an oven for 15 to 20 minutes, or until the outer surface of the food becomes golden brown. Then, lower the heat to 163°C to 177°C (325°F to 350°F) to finish the cooking process.

A cooking technique which derives its name from the French verb for jumping. Sauté is a dry-heat cooking method that involves cooking a small amount of fat in a hot pan while tossing ingredients around. It is also used to enhance the flavors in a dish by browning the surface area of food. Ingredients must be stirred regularly with a utensil throughout the sautéing process to ensure all ingredients are evenly exposed to the heat source.

A fast and fresh way to cook: bite-sized pieces of food are tossed and turned in a little hot oil in a wok over high heat, and in five minutes or less, the work is done. Vegetables emerge crisp and bright; meats are flavorful, tender, and well seared.

A method of cooking that uses a heavy pan containing a moderate amount of fat for cooking foods over moderate heat. The fat helps prevent the fried food from sticking to the pan. Food is generally cooked until brown on one side, then turned over so it can be cooked until brown on the other side.
A process in which food is completely submerged (or only partially submerged, i.e., doughnuts) in hot oil whose temperature is typically between 350°F (177°C) and 375°F (191°C).

A cooking technique that involves cooking in oil, generally in a frying pan. It is usually used to cook small pieces of meat or fish that are generally covered in flour or some type of batter. In shallow frying, the pan is filled two-thirds of the way with oil so that the food will be only partly submerged.

terms.term: Combination of Dry Heat and Moist Heat Cooking Techniques
terms.definition: Useful for tough yet flavorful cuts of meat. The combination techniques create tenderness in the meat. Examples of the combination technique are braising and stewing.

Comes from the French word braiser, meaning a technique that uses both dry heat and moist heat cooking. Braising is used to tenderize tough cuts of meat, such as shank, shoulder, and round. It is a long and slow cooking process that helps break down the connective tissue in the meat, making it tender and combined with flavor sauce. The meat is first seared at a high temperature to brown it, then removed from the pot while onion, leeks, garlic, and other aromatics are added. Liquid, such as stocks, sauce, or water, is added to help deglaze the bottom of the pot. After deglazing, the browned meat is placed back in, but the liquid should not rise over the meat. The mixture is brought to a boil, then the heat is lowered to cook slowly for an extended amount of time.

Another combination cooking technique. The cooking time for stewing is much shorter than braising because the food item in stewing is cut into smaller portions. The cooking process for stewing is the same as braising, wherein meat is first seared at a high temperature. Tender cuts of meat are not stewed, to avoid toughening the meat. It is removed from the pot while onion, leeks, garlic, and other aromatics are added, then liquid, such as stocks, sauce, or water, is added to help deglaze the bottom of the pot. Once deglazed, the browned meat is placed back into the pot, and all ingredients are submerged in liquid.

sets.name: Functions and Binary Numbers
sets.description: Functions (domain, range, and their operations) and binary numbers.

terms.definition: An equation that relates or connects one set into other sets, transforming an input (the domain) into an output (the range).

sets.name: Cordillera Administrative Region
sets.description: The provinces and capitals of the Cordillera Administrative Region, with its attractions, foods and delicacies, and festivals.

terms.term: 6 Provinces of the Cordillera Administrative Region and Their Capitals

terms.definition: Serves as the regional center of the Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR). Widely known as the "Summer Capital of the Philippines" because of its cool climate.
Known as the "Salad Bowl of the Philippines" due to its thriving vegetable farming industry, which supplies a large portion of the country's highland vegetables.

An attraction in Apayao. Originally constructed in 1684 and designed with fortress-like features to protect Spanish colonizers from local resistance. Abandoned in 1815 due to persistent attacks by the Isneg people, one of the major Indigenous groups in the province. Spanish authorities regained partial control of the area in 1891.

An attraction in Abra. Showcases the long-standing weaving tradition of the province, where local artisans produce textiles using traditional handlooms. Visitors can observe the weaving process and directly purchase locally made products.

An attraction in Kalinga. Widely recognized for its strong indigenous heritage and scenic mountainous surroundings. Home to Apo Whang-Od and, due to its remote location, has maintained much of its traditional lifestyle.
A National Living Treasure from Buscalan Village, Kalinga, known for preserving the traditional tattooing practice called "batok."
The traditional tattooing practice preserved in Buscalan Village, which symbolizes bravery, identity, and social status in Kalinga culture.

An attraction in Kalinga. Famous for its natural ridge formation that resembles a sleeping woman, which is why it is widely known as the "Sleeping Beauty Mountain." One of Kalinga's most recognizable natural landmarks and a contributor to its growing ecotourism industry.

An attraction in Mountain Province. An ancient burial tradition practiced by the Igorot people, where coffins are placed along limestone cliffs to bring the deceased closer to ancestral spirits. Traditionally, elderly individuals prepare their own coffins, while families assist when necessary.

terms.term: 6 Aspects of the Kankanaey Burial Tradition

terms.definition: Only full-blooded Kankanaey elders who are married, have children and grandchildren, and die peacefully of old age may receive a cliffside burial.
Elders traditionally carve their own pine-log coffin while still alive. The coffin is made short because the body will be placed in a fetal position.
The deceased is placed on a death chair for a 3-6 day vigil. The body is preserved through continuous smoking, while a village elder performs rituals and animal offerings.
The body is wrapped in a traditional woven cloth and placed in a fetal position, symbolizing a return to the beginning of life.
Young men carry the body to the cliff, believing this passes on the deceased's wisdom and blessings. Skilled climbers then secure the coffin to the cliff face.
The Kankanaey believe elevated coffins bring the soul closer to heaven and ancestors, while also protecting the remains from animals and natural hazards and preserving farmland.

An attraction in Mountain Province. A traditional stone structure used as a communal gathering place where elders discuss social, political, and spiritual concerns. A central fireplace symbolizes unity, while wooden poles are used to display animal offerings during rituals. It reflects the indigenous governance system and the importance of collective decision-making in Cordilleran society.

An attraction in Ifugao. Among the most iconic cultural landscapes in the country, believed to have been carved by the Ifugao people more than 2,000 years ago. They demonstrate advanced indigenous knowledge in engineering and sustainable agriculture, and are often referred to as the "Eighth Wonder of the World."

An attraction in Benguet. An open-air museum and art colony designed to replicate a traditional Cordilleran village, featuring reconstructed, authentic Ifugao and Kalinga huts. It functions as a living museum where visitors can learn about indigenous lifestyles, artistic traditions, and local craftsmanship.

An attraction in Benguet. One of the most recognized religious landmarks in the region and one of the largest churches in Baguio City. During World War II, it served as an evacuation center for civilians, and it was the only major building to survive the devastating carpet-bombing of Baguio City during the war. Its elevated location provides a panoramic view of the city.

An attraction in Benguet. The official summer residence of the President of the Philippines. Originally built in 1908 as the residence of American Governor-Generals, and declared a National Historic Landmark in 2009. It has reopened to the public as the Presidential Museum after a major renovation.

Deeply shaped by the region's agricultural traditions and cool mountain climate, commonly using locally available ingredients such as rice, root crops, pork, and native plants. Traditional cooking methods often include fermenting, curing, and smoking meat to help preserve it for longer periods. Because the Cordillera is a mountainous inland region with limited access to seafood, communities relied more on livestock such as pigs and chickens.

A delicacy of Apayao. A traditional chicken dish prepared through a cultural ritual process, cooked with native spices and known for its smoky flavor. The chicken is traditionally tapped gently before slaughter, a practice believed to improve the flavor and performed as part of indigenous rituals.

A delicacy of Abra. A noodle dish made with fresh egg noodles, pork, and vegetables, known for its rich broth and savory flavor. The noodles are traditionally handmade, giving them a firm and chewy texture.

A delicacy of Kalinga. A traditional rice cake (kakanin) made from glutinous rice and local ingredients, commonly prepared during gatherings, festivals, and cultural celebrations. It is served as a dessert because it is coated with a rich, sweet coconut caramel (latik or ladok) made from coconut cream and sugar. Its name comes from its shape, as the sticky rice dough is molded to resemble a human tongue before being wrapped and cooked.

A delicacy of Mountain Province. A traditional rice wine made from fermented glutinous rice through a natural fermentation process using indigenous yeast. It is an essential part of indigenous ceremonies such as weddings, thanksgiving rituals, harvest festivals, and peace agreements. Offering it to guests is a sign of hospitality, friendship, and respect.

A delicacy of Ifugao. A traditional blood sausage made from pork blood, meat, fat, and local spices, known for its rich, savory flavor. Commonly served as a viand, usually grilled, boiled, or fried and eaten with rice. It reflects the Ifugao tradition of using every part of the pig.

A delicacy of Benguet. A traditional preserved pork cured with salt and smoked or sun-dried, developed as a meat preservation method before refrigeration. Commonly used as a seasoning to add a smoky, salty, and savory flavor to soups and vegetable dishes, and can also be grilled or cooked and served as a viand. An important ingredient in Cordilleran dishes such as Pinikpikan.

terms.term: 6 Foods and Delicacies of the Cordillera Administrative Region

terms.definition: A festival of Abra. Held March 6-9 to recognize bamboo as one of the province's most important natural resources. It coincides with the founding anniversary of Abra and features street dancing, bamboo craft exhibits, and cultural presentations, highlighting the creativity and skills of local artisans who use bamboo in various products and industries.

A festival of Apayao. Held February 1-14, with the main celebration on February 14, as both a thanksgiving ritual for a bountiful harvest and a commemoration of the province's founding anniversary. It honors the traditions of the Isneg people through cultural performances, music, and dances.

A festival of Benguet. Held in February in Baguio City and widely known as the Flower Festival due to its colorful floral floats and street dancing performances. It began as a symbol of recovery after the 1990 Luzon earthquake and has grown into a major tourism event.

A festival of Ifugao. Held in April, usually every 3 years in Banaue, as a cultural thanksgiving event that highlights the traditions of the Ifugao people. It features indigenous games, rituals, and cultural performances that showcase community values and identity.

A festival of Kalinga. Held February 13-16 to preserve and promote the rich cultural traditions of the Kalinga people. It is inspired by the ullalim epic chant, which tells stories of heroism, ancestry, and community values, and includes indigenous dances, rituals, and performances.

A festival of Mountain Province. Held the first week of April as part of the founding anniversary of the province. The word "lang-ay" means unity and sharing, reflecting cooperation among indigenous communities. It promotes appreciation of cultural heritage while supporting tourism and local economic development.

terms.term: 6 Festivals of the Cordillera Administrative Region

terms.definition: Located in Intramuros. Oldest stone church in the Philippines, completed in 1607. UNESCO World Heritage Site under Baroque Churches of the Philippines. Known for its Baroque architecture, ornate interiors, and religious artifacts.

Built in 1571 by the Spanish as a military defense fortress. Served as the prison of Dr. José Rizal before his execution in 1896. Now a preserved historical site and museum showcasing colonial history.
One of the largest urban parks in Asia. Site of Dr. Jose Rizal's execution and location of the Rizal Monument. Serves as a national landmark and public recreational space.

33-hectare ecological park near the La Mesa Watershed. Offers activities such as nature walks, bird watching, and outdoor recreation. Promotes environmental conservation and biodiversity awareness.
A rich noodle dish with thick sauce, seafood, and toppings, known for its distinct orange color and flavor.
A flaky pastry filled with sweet bean paste, originating from Tipas, Taguig.
A layered rice cake made from glutinous rice flour, coconut milk, and sugar.
Affordable skewered snacks served with savory sauces, popular in urban areas.

Held on January 9. A major religious celebration held in Quiapo, Manila, honoring a revered devotional image. Millions of devotees participate in the Traslación. Many participants walk barefoot as a sign of deep faith and devotion.

Held January–February (varies annually). Widely celebrated in Binondo, Manila, known as the oldest Chinatown in the world. Features colorful dragon and lion dances, fireworks displays, and cultural performances. Highlights the strong Chinese-Filipino cultural influence and the multicultural identity of the National Capital Region.

sets.description: The provinces and capitals of the Ilocos Region, with its attractions, foods and delicacies, and festivals.

terms.definition: An attraction in Ilocos Norte. Also known as San Agustin Church. Recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Characterized by thick coral stone walls and massive buttresses designed to withstand earthquakes.
An attraction in Ilocos Norte. A centuries-old bell tower that mysteriously sinks into the ground over time; a symbol of Laoag's Spanish colonial past.

An attraction in Ilocos Sur. A well-preserved heritage street in Vigan City. Features cobblestone roads lined with Spanish-era houses. Showcases antique lamps and traditional horse-drawn carriages (kalesa).

An attraction in Ilocos Sur. A historic bell tower located on a hill overlooking Vigan. Part of the Saint Augustine Parish Church complex. Built in the 16th century and used as a watchtower during the Spanish colonial period.
An attraction in Ilocos Sur. A popular tourist attraction in Vigan City. Owned by former governor Luis "Chavit" Singson. Features a mini zoo, safari gallery, and recreational facilities.
An attraction in La Union. One of the well-known natural attractions in La Union. Located in San Gabriel and accessible through trekking. Popular for swimming and nature trips.

An attraction in La Union. One of the largest Taoist temples in the Philippines, and the first Taoist temple in the Philippines. Built in 1975 with the support of the local Chinese-Filipino community.
An attraction in Pangasinan. Located in Alaminos City. Composed of 124 islands scattered across Lingayen Gulf. Known for island hopping, snorkeling, and beach activities.

An attraction in Pangasinan. A major Roman Catholic pilgrimage site. Officially known as the Minor Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary of Manaoag. Devotees visit the shrine due to its long-standing religious significance.
A delicacy of Ilocos Norte. A savory pastry filled with vegetables, egg, and Ilocos longganisa. Known for its crispy orange-colored rice flour crust.
A delicacy of Ilocos Sur. A garlicky and slightly sour native sausage. Commonly served with garlic rice and fried egg.
A delicacy of La Union. A fresh salad of live shrimp mixed with vinegar, onions, and tomatoes.
A delicacy of Pangasinan. A soft, bite-sized steamed rice cake. Made from rice flour, sugar, and yeast, known for its slightly sticky texture.

terms.term: 4 Foods and Delicacies of the Ilocos Region

Held every February 10 in Laoag City, this festival honors St. William the Hermit through street dancing, cultural performances, and religious activities. Its name is inspired by a traditional Ilocano folk song which reflects the rich heritage of the community.

A festival of Ilocos Sur. Celebrated every January 22 in Vigan City, this festival showcases the famous Ilocos longganisa through lively street dancing and fun eating contests that highlight the region's well-loved delicacy.

A social event of La Union. Surfers from all around the world come together for this yearly event every January. It supports local tourism and businesses while promoting La Union as a premier surfing destination.

A festival of Pangasinan. Held each year in Dagupan City from April 16 to May 4 to commemorate the abundance of milkfish production in the area. It includes dancing, fluvial processions, and grill parties attracting lots of tourists.
